label: Accordion
summary: A stack of panels whose headers the person opens to show or hide their content.
overview:
Every panel header is in the Tab order; the Up and Down arrow keys also move focus between the headers, Home and End jump to the first and last. Disabled panels are skipped. Without multiple, opening a panel (by the person or by setting open) closes the others.

Items fire open and close.
example: ```html Panel 1 Summary text Content Panel 2 Content ```

attributes.description:
Whether multiple panels can be expanded simultaneously.
When `false` (default), expanding one panel collapses all others.

attributes.name: variant
attributes.description:
Variant for the accordion.
`'default'` renders panels with a subtle background on expand and dividers between items.
`'flat'` renders panels without borders or background changes — suitable for use inside cards.

attributes.name: leading-toggle
attributes.description:
When `true`, the toggle icon is placed at the leading start of the header.
When `false` (default), the icon is placed at the trailing end.

label: AI Badge
summary: Marks a value, draft or text as made by the assistant, says why, and can clear it in one action.
overview:
The one marker for AI output in Peacock (ADR-030002). Put it beside anything the assistant made until a person accepts it:

  • suggested (default): a value the person hasn't accepted, such as a field the assistant filled in.
  • draft: a record or text waiting to be confirmed, such as an incident the assistant prepared.
  • generated: read-only output, such as a summary. Shown as colored text without a container.

reason says why, in a sentence: it shows in a tooltip on hover or keyboard focus and is read as the badge's description. dismissible adds a clear button that fires dismiss; the app then removes the suggestion, discards the draft or hides the summary.

icon-only keeps just the sparkle where there is no room for the label, such as a narrow field: the label is still read and shows in the tooltip. Fields switch to it on their own when they are narrow.

When AI is off for the page (setPeacockAi({ enabled: false })) the badge renders nothing, so a page that still passes AI state in never shows a stale marker.

The label is always text, never only the color or the sparkle. Replace it with the default slot, for example "Summary by the assistant".
slot: - The label, instead of the default one for the kind.
cssprop: --ai-badge-color - Text and sparkle color.
fires: dismiss - Fired when the clear button is pressed.

label: AI Summary
summary: A summary written by the assistant, marked as such, with its sources, why it says what it says, and a way to hide it.
overview:
Use it where the assistant sums something up: the day's items on Home, a long discussion, the answer to an administrator's question, a digest of notifications (ADR-030002). The facts come from the platform; the summary puts them into words and cites the records with [1](cite:id) links and citations.

Give the Markdown in value. While it is being written, show loading (placeholder lines and status), then streaming as the text arrives. With error it says the summary couldn't be written and offers Try again; whatever it sits on is unaffected.

It is marked "By the assistant" (badge-label changes it). The header has Try again (regenerate) and Hide (dismiss); the footer has a good or bad rating (feedback) and the why slot, for a link such as "Why these items?".

variant="inline" is a one-line insight with a sparkle, for the insight slot of wc-stat and the charts or a list's header: no headline, actions or footer.

It renders nothing while AI is off for the page; the page under it must make sense without it.
slot: why - A link that explains the summary, such as "Why these items?".
cssprop: --ai-summary-background - Background of the card.
fires: feedback - The person rated the summary, or took the rating back.
example:
```html
<wc-ai-summary headline="For you today" value="- Your leave on 13 November is still waiting[1](cite:lv_7)"></wc-ai-summary>
```

label: Alert
summary: A short, prominent message in the page, with an optional icon, action and close button.
overview:
An alert is part of the page. For a transient message use wc-snackbar, or wc-notification-manager for a queue of them.

An alert is not a live region by default, so an alert that is on the page when it loads is read in the normal reading order and not announced. Set live="polite" (status) or live="assertive" (alert) on an alert you add or change while the page is in use.

With dismissible a close button fires a cancelable close event with reason: 'action' and then hides the alert (sets hidden). Call preventDefault() on the event to keep it, for example to remove it yourself.
slot: action - Buttons at the end of the alert, for example `<wc-button variant="text" size="sm">`.
fires: close - Fired, cancelable, when the close button is pressed. The alert hides unless the event is cancelled.
cssprop: --alert-border-radius - Border radius of the alert surface.
example:
```html
<wc-alert intent="warning" dismissible description="Your trial ends in 3 days.">
  <wc-button slot="action" variant="text" size="sm">Upgrade</wc-button>
</wc-alert>
```

label: Anchor Nav
summary: "On this page" links to the sections of a long page, highlighting the one in view.
overview:
An anchor nav lists the sections of a long settings or documentation page and marks the one being read. Point for at the element holding the content and it lists its h2 and h3 headings (an h3 nested under the h2 before it), using each heading's text as the link and its id as the target; a heading without an id gets one made from its text. It follows headings added, removed or renamed later. Or set items to { id, label, level? } objects, for sections that are not headings or labels that differ from them; items wins when both are set.

The link of the section in view has aria-current="location". A section is in view once its top passes the first third of the scroll container; at the very end of the page the last section is current even when it is too short to reach that line. The nav fires change when the current section changes.

Pressing a link scrolls its section into view, smoothly unless the person asks for reduced motion, and moves focus to the section's heading (giving it tabindex="-1" when it is not focusable), so keyboard and screen reader users continue reading from there. Set update-hash to also put the section in the address bar with history.replaceState(), without adding a history entry. Links are real #id links, so they can be copied or opened in a new tab.

The sections may scroll inside an element rather than the page: the nav uses the nearest scrolling ancestor of the sections (such as a wc-scroll-area), or the element that scroll-container selects. Set scroll-margin-top on the headings when a sticky header covers the top of the scroll container.

The nav is a nav landmark named "On this page" (label to change it); headline shows a visible title, which then names the landmark. It does not stick in place on its own: put it in a sidebar and give it position: sticky and top when it should stay visible while the page scrolls. Call refresh() after replacing the content wholesale or moving the sections.
fires: change - Dispatched when the section in view changes. `value` is its id.
cssprop: --anchor-nav-track-color - Color of the line along the links.
example:
```html
<wc-anchor-nav id="settings-nav"></wc-anchor-nav>
<script>
  document.querySelector('#settings-nav').items = [
    { id: 'profile', label: 'Profile' },
    { id: 'notifications', label: 'Notifications' },
    { id: 'email', label: 'Email', level: 2 },
  ];
</script>
```

label: App Bar
summary: A top app bar for page-level navigation and actions.
overview:
The app bar component implements the top app bar pattern. It provides a consistent header for screens, housing a navigation icon, a page title/headline, and optional trailing action icons.

Four size variants are available: small (64dp, single-row), center-aligned (64dp, centred headline), medium (112dp, headline below the row), and large (152dp, large headline).

Use the start slot for a navigation icon (e.g. a hamburger or back button), the default slot for the headline text, and the end slot for action icon buttons.

The app bar is not a landmark on its own, so it can sit in cards, panes and dialogs. For the page's banner, put it in a <header> element.
slot: end - Action icon buttons placed at the end of the bar.
cssprop: --app-bar-shadow - Box-shadow applied when the bar is scrolled / elevated.
example:
```html
<!-- Large app bar -->
<wc-app-bar variant="large">
  <wc-icon-button slot="start" variant="text"><wc-icon name="arrow_back"></wc-icon></wc-icon-button>
  Large Headline
  <wc-icon-button slot="end" variant="text"><wc-icon name="more_vert"></wc-icon></wc-icon-button>
</wc-app-bar>
```

label: App Shell
summary: The page frame of an app: header, navigation, main content, side panel and footer.
overview:
App shell lays out a whole app screen at the full viewport height (100dvh). The header slot (usually a wc-app-bar) stays at the top, the navigation slot (usually a wc-navigation-drawer) sits at the start, the optional aside slot at the end, and the footer slot at the bottom. Only the main region scrolls.

The shell supplies the page landmarks: a <header>, a <main>, an <aside> and a <footer>. The navigation drawer, rail and bar are navigation landmarks themselves, so the shell only marks the navigation region as one when the slotted content is not. A visually hidden Skip to main content link is the first focusable element.

When the shell is narrower than breakpoint (840px by default), the navigation moves into a modal drawer that slides in from the start edge. The shell renders a menu button before the header to open it (hide-menu-button hides it, for apps that call toggleNavigation() from their own button). Choosing an item, Escape and a click on the scrim close it. navigation-open reflects that drawer's state.

On wider screens, navigation-collapsed narrows the navigation to rail width. Put a wc-navigation-rail in the rail slot to show it instead of the drawer while collapsed; without one, the drawer is clipped to the rail width.

A wc-navigation-drawer in the shell keeps variant="standard" and open: the shell moves it into its own modal drawer on narrow screens.

fires: close - Dispatched when the modal navigation drawer closes: Escape, a scrim click, choosing an item, or `hideNavigation()` (and widening the shell past the breakpoint).

cssprop: --app-shell-modal-navigation-width - Width of the modal drawer. Defaults to 22.5rem.

label: Assistant Panel
summary: The assistant's side panel: a header that says whose access it uses, the conversation, the composer and a reminder to check drafts.
overview:
The frame of a conversation with the assistant (ADR-030002). Put a wc-chat-thread in the default slot and a wc-prompt-input in the composer slot. supporting-text says whose access the assistant uses, such as "Acting as Alan Turing, with your access"; below the composer a line reminds that the assistant can be wrong (replace it with the disclaimer slot).

The header has New conversation (new-conversation) and Close (close). With variant="standard" (default) the panel fills its container, such as wc-app-shell's aside slot; with variant="modal" it opens as a modal sheet from the end edge, for small screens, with open, show(), hide() and toggle(); it opens with the composer focused.

Like every marker of the assistant, the panel renders nothing while AI is off for the page, so a page that still mounts it shows no stale assistant.

cssprop: --assistant-panel-width - Width of the modal sheet.
fires: open - A modal panel opened.

```html
  <wc-chat-thread></wc-chat-thread>
  <wc-prompt-input slot="composer"></wc-prompt-input>
</wc-assistant-panel>
```

Steps come from the platform's calls, so a person can see what an answer is based on, and a step their access did not allow says so (ADR-000007: the assistant acts as the person using it).

overview:
The avatar shows the image at src. Without one, or when the image fails to load, it shows the initials of name (the first letters of its first and last words), and without a name a person icon.

The avatar is named by label, or else name: the image gets it as alt, the initials and the icon as role="img" with aria-label. An avatar with neither is decorative and hidden from assistive technology.

Put wc-avatar elements inside. They overlap, each separated from the next by a ring in the surface color, and stack from the start edge, so from the right in RTL. size (sm, md, lg) is passed down to every avatar.

With max, the group shows the first max avatars and then a +N button for the rest; its accessible name is "N more". Pressing it opens a popover that lists the hidden avatars by name. Without max, or with fewer avatars, every avatar shows and there is no button.

label: Badge
summary: A small count or dot on an icon or a label, such as the number of unread messages.
overview:
A badge shows a count, or with dot (or no value) a small dot. A number above max (default 99) shows as 99+.

A dot alone means nothing to a screen reader, so it is hidden from assistive technology unless it has a label. Give a count a label such as "3 unread messages" when the number alone is not enough. When the badge sits on an icon button, put the full meaning in the button's aria-label instead (for example "Inbox, 3 unread") and leave the badge without a label.

intent (info, success, warning, danger) sets its color; without it the badge uses the theme's badge color.
cssprop: --badge-text-color - Controls the color of the count.
example:
```html

<wc-badge value="120" label="120 unread messages"></wc-badge>
<wc-badge dot intent="success"></wc-badge>
```

label: Banner
summary: A full-width message at the top of the app or a page, such as a maintenance window, an ending trial or a lost connection.
overview:
Pick the message component by where the message belongs and how long it matters:

  • Banner: about the whole app or page and true until something changes (maintenance tonight, trial ends in 3 days, you are offline). It spans the full width above the content and stays until the condition ends or the person dismisses it. Show one at a time.
  • wc-alert: about one part of the content, shown in place beside it (a form section that failed to save, a setting with a caveat).
  • wc-snackbar: brief feedback on something the person just did (message sent, item deleted, with Undo); it floats and goes away by itself.

The banner takes the alert's vocabulary: intent (info, success, warning, danger; neutral when unset) sets the color and icon, headline is the bold lead-in, the message is the default slot or description, and the action slot takes one or two buttons. With sticky it stays at the top of its scroll container while the page scrolls.

With dismissible a close button fires a cancelable close event with reason: 'action' and then hides the banner (sets hidden). Add dismiss-key to remember the dismissal in localStorage (under wc-banner:<key>): a banner with a key that was dismissed before starts hidden. Change the key (for example maintenance-2026-11-20) to show a new message again. When storage is blocked the banner simply shows again on the next visit.

A banner is not a live region by default, so one that is there when the page loads is read in reading order, not announced. Set live="polite" (status) or live="assertive" (alert, for urgent news such as a lost connection) on a banner you add or change while the page is in use.
slot: action - One or two buttons, for example `<wc-button variant="text" size="sm">`.
fires: close - Fired, cancelable, when the close button is pressed. The banner hides (and remembers it under `dismiss-key`) unless the event is cancelled.
cssprop: --banner-z-index - Stacking order while `sticky`. Defaults to `var(--z-index-banner, 10)`.
example:
```html
<wc-banner intent="danger" live="assertive" sticky headline="Connection lost">
  Changes are saved on this device until you are back online.
</wc-banner>
```

customElement.description: The localStorage key a `dismiss-key` is stored under.

label: Bottom Sheet
summary: A panel that slides up from the bottom of the screen with extra content, either modal over the page or alongside it.
overview:
The sheet renders a native <dialog>. The modal variant (the default) opens it with showModal(): it renders in the browser's top layer above the page, with a scrim; the rest of the page is inert and does not scroll; focus moves to the first element with autofocus inside it and returns where it was when the sheet closes. Escape and a click on the scrim close it (no-light-dismiss keeps it open on scrim clicks).

The drag handle closes the sheet when dragged down, clicked, or pressed with Enter or Space.

The standard variant opens the dialog with show(): it is not modal and stays in the page flow at the end of its container.

label: Breadcrumb
summary: A trail of links that shows where the current page sits in the site and leads back up it.
overview:
• Breadcrumbs provide a trail for users to follow back to the starting or entry point.
  • They help users understand their current location within the site hierarchy.
  • Follows WCAG 2.1 guidelines for accessible navigation landmarks: the breadcrumb is a <nav> landmark named by label (by default Peacock's breadcrumb string) holding an ordered list, and each wc-breadcrumb-item is one of its list items.
  • Mark the page the user is on with current on its item: it renders as text with aria-current="page".

label: Button Group
summary: A row of related buttons or icon buttons that share one size, color and style.
overview:
Put wc-button or wc-icon-button elements inside. The group passes its size (sm by default), and its color and variant when set, to every button, overriding what the buttons set themselves.

By default the buttons sit with a small gap between them. With connected they sit 2px apart with rounded outer corners, for a set such as bold, italic and underline toggles.

The group is layout only: it adds no group role, keyboard handling or selection, so each button keeps its own focus stop and toggle state. For choosing one or several options from a set use wc-segmented-button-group.
example:
```html
<wc-button-group connected>
 <wc-icon-button toggle="true" shape="wide" selected>
   <wc-icon name="format_bold"></wc-icon>
 </wc-icon-button>
 <wc-icon-button toggle="true" shape="wide">
   <wc-icon name="format_italic"></wc-icon>
 </wc-icon-button>
 <wc-icon-button toggle="true" shape="wide">
   <wc-icon name="format_underlined"></wc-icon>
 </wc-icon-button>
</wc-button-group>
```

Button size.
Possible values are `"xs"`, `"sm"`, `"md"`, `"lg"`, `"xl"`. Defaults to `"sm"`.

attributes.name: connected
attributes.description:
Layout variant of the button group.
`"standard"` shows buttons with a small gap between them.
`"connected"` places buttons with a 2px gap;
rounded outer corners and middle buttons keep standard rounded corners.
Defaults to `"standard"`.

attributes.description:
Color applied to all buttons in the group.
Possible values are `"primary"`, `"success"`, `"danger"`, `"warning"`, `"surface"`, `"on-surface"`.

attributes.name: variant
attributes.description:

Possible values are `"filled"`, `"tonal"`, `"outlined"`.

label: Calendar
summary: A calendar that shows events by day, week or month, with controls to move between periods.
overview:
Pass events as the events property; each has a start, end, title and optional palette color. The day and week views lay timed events out in a column per day, with events lasting a day or more in a row above; the month view shows six weeks. available-views sets the views offered in the header's segmented buttons, and view the one shown.

The header has a Today button, previous and next buttons and the current date, which is a polite live region. previous(), next() and today() do the same from code; each fires date-change. The date shown is date (an ISO string) or contextDate (a Date), kept in step. Choosing a day number in a column view switches to the day view and fires view-change and date-change.

Events are buttons, chosen with a click, Enter or Space, which fire event-click. With events-readonly they are shown but cannot be focused or clicked. loading shows a progress bar and marks the calendar busy. first-day sets the week start (else the locale's), timezone the zone the current time is shown in, and locale the language of names and times.

overview:
Rendered by wc-calendar; not meant to be used on its own.

The view is a region labelled with the dates it shows. Day numbers in the header are buttons that open the day; events are buttons labelled with their title and time, or notes that cannot be focused when events-readonly is set. Events lasting a day or more are shown in a row above the hours.

label: Calendar Month View
summary: The calendar's month view, six weeks of days with the events on each.
overview:
Rendered by wc-calendar; not meant to be used on its own.

The month is a read-only ARIA grid labelled with the month and year: one row per week, one gridcell per day labelled with its full date. Each event is owned (aria-owns) by the cell of the day it starts on in that week. Events are buttons labelled with their title and time, or notes that cannot be focused when events-readonly is set.

label: Card
summary: A surface that groups content and actions about one subject.
overview:
A card is elevated (the default), filled or outlined. It adds no padding of its own: put text in wc-card-content, which can sit next to edge-to-edge media.

Set actionable to make the whole card a single button that fires click, or href (with target, rel and download) to make it a link. The content of an actionable or link card is inert, so don't put buttons or links inside one; use a plain card with its own actions instead. throttle-delay throttles activation.

disabled dims the card and makes its content inert; an actionable or link card also stops responding to clicks and leaves the tab order. With disabled-reason it stays focusable and screen readers read the reason with it.

label: Carousel
summary: A row of slides shown one or a few at a time, with previous and next buttons and pickers.
overview:
Carousel shows its children as slides, per-view at a time, for screenshots on a product page or a row of testimonials. The slides scroll with snap points, so touch swipe, trackpads and the scroll wheel work as they do anywhere else, and previous, next and picker buttons sit under them. With more than seven pages a "3 of 9" counter replaces the pickers.

Each slide is never narrower than 15rem, so a carousel of three drops to two and then one as its container narrows. Slides out of view are inert, so Tab never reaches a link the person cannot see.

Slides do not move on their own unless you set autoplay, and then a button to stop them comes first in the controls. Rotation pauses while the pointer rests on the carousel or focus is inside it, stops for good when the person uses any control, and does not start at all when the person asks for reduced motion.

label: CB Rule
summary: One condition row in a condition builder: a drag handle, the slotted field, operator and value controls, and a remove button.
overview:
Drag the handle to reorder the rule, or to move it into another group. With the handle focused, ArrowUp and ArrowDown move the rule within its group, ArrowRight moves it into the group beside it (the one above, else the one below) and ArrowLeft moves it out of its group; each move is announced. In the builder's value a rule reports its own value property when set, else the values of its slotted controls (keyed by name when every control has one).

label: Area Chart
summary: A line chart with the area under each line filled, optionally stacked to show parts of a total over time.
overview:
An area chart is a wc-chart-line with each area filled with a fading gradient of its series color, and it takes the same data and attributes: data rows, category-key for the category field, and config for the series (every numeric field of the first row when omitted). Use a line chart when the series overlap so much that fills would hide each other.

  • stacked places the series on top of each other, so the top line shows the total.
  • curve joins the points monotone (smooth, the default), linear or step; show-dots draws a dot at every point.
  • hide-grid, hide-category-axis and hide-value-axis remove the gridlines and axis labels.
  • height sets the plot height in pixels (300 by default); the width follows the container.

Hovering or focusing a category shows a tooltip with every visible series' value (hide-tooltip turns it off). The legend shows for more than one series by default (legend: auto, show or hide); each entry is a toggle button that hides or shows its series, and hovering one highlights it. valueFormatter formats values in tooltips and on the axis.

The plot is focusable. The arrow keys move through the categories (Left and Right follow the reading direction), Home and End jump to the first and last, Escape clears the focus, and Enter or Space fires select. Each move is announced through a polite live region, and a visually hidden table holds the data for screen readers. Give the chart a label to name it.

loading shows a skeleton, and the empty slot shows when there is no data. Marks animate unless disable-animation is set or the user prefers reduced motion.

label: Bar Chart
summary: Compares values across categories with vertical or horizontal bars, grouped or stacked by series.
overview:
Set data to an array of rows and category-key to the field that holds each row's category label. config names the series fields, with an optional label and color for each; without it every numeric field of the first row becomes a series. Several series sit side by side in each category. Use wc-chart-line for a trend over ordered categories such as time, and wc-chart-pie for the parts of a single whole.

  • orientation: vertical (the default) draws columns; horizontal draws bars from the left, which suits long category labels.
  • stacked stacks the series in each category instead of placing them side by side. Negative values stack below zero.
  • show-values prints each bar's value at its end, or each stack's total when stacked.
  • hide-grid, hide-category-axis and hide-value-axis remove the gridlines and axis labels. Category labels are thinned out when they would overlap.
  • height sets the plot height in pixels (300 by default); the width follows the container.

Hovering or focusing a category highlights its bars and shows a tooltip with every visible series' value (hide-tooltip turns it off). The legend shows for more than one series by default (legend: auto, show or hide); each entry is a toggle button that hides or shows its series, and hovering one highlights it. valueFormatter formats values in tooltips, value labels and on the axis; by default they use the locale's number format, compact on the axis.

The plot is focusable. The arrow keys move through the categories (Left and Right follow the reading direction), Home and End jump to the first and last, Escape clears the focus, and Enter or Space fires select, whose detail includes series when only one series is visible. Each move is announced through a polite live region, and a visually hidden table holds the data for screen readers. Give the chart a label to name it.

loading shows a skeleton, and the empty slot shows when there is no data. Bars grow in and animate on data changes unless disable-animation is set or the user prefers reduced motion.

label: Doughnut Chart
summary: A pie chart with a hole that shows the total, or the hovered slice, in its centre.
overview:
A doughnut chart is a wc-chart-pie with a hole, and takes the same data: an array of slices, each with a unique name, a value, and an optional label and color.

  • The centre shows the total of the visible slices with a caption, or the value and label of the hovered or focused slice. center-label sets the caption (by default the localized string "Total"), and the center slot replaces the content.
  • inner-radius sets the size of the hole as a fraction of the radius, 0.62 by default and at most 0.9. At 0 there is no hole and no centre content.
  • show-labels prints each slice's percentage inside it when the slice is big enough.
  • height sets the plot height in pixels (300 by default); the width follows the container.

Hovering or focusing a slice pulls it out, dims the others and shows a tooltip with its value and share of the visible total (hide-tooltip turns it off). The legend shows by default (legend: auto, show or hide); each entry is a toggle button that hides or shows its slice. valueFormatter formats the values.

The plot is focusable. The arrow keys move through the slices (Left and Right follow the reading direction), Home and End jump to the first and last, Escape clears the focus, and Enter or Space fires select. Each move is announced through a polite live region, and a visually hidden table lists each slice's name, value and share for screen readers. Give the chart a label to name it.

loading shows a skeleton, and the empty slot shows when no slice has a value above zero. Slices animate unless disable-animation is set or the user prefers reduced motion.
example:
```html
<wc-chart-doughnut label="Visitors by browser" center-label="Visitors"></wc-chart-doughnut>
<script>
  document.querySelector('wc-chart-doughnut').data = [
    { name: 'chrome', label: 'Chrome', value: 275 },
    { name: 'safari', label: 'Safari', value: 200 },
    { name: 'firefox', label: 'Firefox', value: 187 },
  ];
</script>
```

label: Pie Chart
summary: Shows how parts make up a whole. Best with a handful of slices.
overview:
Set data to an array of slices, each with a unique name, a value, and an optional label and color. Slices keep the order they are given in. Use wc-chart-doughnut to show the total in the centre, and wc-chart-bar when there are many parts or they need to be compared precisely.

  • show-labels prints each slice's percentage inside it when the slice is big enough.
  • height sets the plot height in pixels (300 by default); the width follows the container.

Hovering or focusing a slice pulls it out, dims the others and shows a tooltip with its value and share of the visible total (hide-tooltip turns it off). Slices are told apart by the legend, so it shows by default (legend: auto, show or hide); each entry is a toggle button that hides or shows its slice, and percentages are worked out from the visible slices. valueFormatter formats the values.

The plot is focusable. The arrow keys move through the slices (Left and Right follow the reading direction), Home and End jump to the first and last, Escape clears the focus, and Enter or Space fires select. Each move is announced through a polite live region, and a visually hidden table lists each slice's name, value and share for screen readers. Give the chart a label to name it.

loading shows a skeleton, and the empty slot shows when no slice has a value above zero. Slices sweep in and animate on data changes unless disable-animation is set or the user prefers reduced motion.

```html
<wc-chart-pie label="Visitors by browser"></wc-chart-pie>
<script>
  document.querySelector('wc-chart-pie').data = [
    { name: 'chrome', label: 'Chrome', value: 275 },
    { name: 'safari', label: 'Safari', value: 200 },
    { name: 'firefox', label: 'Firefox', value: 187 },
  ];
</script>
```

label: Chat Event
summary: A line in a conversation for something that happened rather than something said, such as "Alan Kay confirmed the rollback".
overview:
Goes in wc-chat-thread between wc-chat-messages. It records what happened to the conversation's subject: a person confirmed a draft, a record changed state, someone joined. The content is the sentence; icon sets the glyph before it, and datetime adds the time after it.

Use a message for anything someone wrote, and an event for anything the platform recorded. Events are not announced as they arrive; the record they describe is what changed.
slot: - What happened. Bold the name of who did it with `<strong>`.
example: ```html Alan Kay confirmed the rollback · policy NET-04 ```

slots.description: What happened. Bold the name of who did it with `<strong>`.

attributes.description: Material Symbols name of the glyph before the text, such as `verified`.

attributes.name: datetime
attributes.description: When it happened, as an ISO 8601 date-time; shown as a time after the text.

attributes.name: locale
attributes.description: Locale for the time; defaults to the nearest `lang`, else the browser's.

label: Chat Message
summary: One turn of a conversation: what the person asked, another person's message, or the assistant's answer with its steps, drafts and sources.
overview:
Put messages in wc-chat-thread. from="user" shows the person's text in a bubble at the end of the line; from="assistant" (default) shows the answer as formatted text; from="participant" shows another person's text, such as a caller's or a teammate's, in a quiet bubble at the start of the line, with their name above it. All take Markdown in value, rendered by wc-markdown, so mentions and [1](cite:id) citations work; give the sources in citations.

Who and when. A line above the message names author and adds channel ("via Teams") and the time of datetime. It shows for a participant, whenever datetime or channel is set, and when the meta slot has content, such as a "Work note" tag. In a one-to-one conversation with the assistant, leave them out and the messages stay bare.

While an answer arrives, set streaming and keep replacing value. Before the first words, a typing indicator shows status, such as "Looking up your laptop…". Put wc-assistant-steps in the steps slot, above the text, and wc-draft-cards in the default slot, below it.

A finished answer has actions: copy, Try again (regenerate) and good or bad (feedback, which toggles feedback). hide-actions removes them. With error the message says the answer failed, with Try again.

Quick replies. suggestions shows the likely next moves as chips under the message ("Promote to major incident", "Why P2?"). Picking one fires suggestion-select; the app sends it and usually clears the list.
slot: footer - Below everything.
cssprop: --chat-message-participant-color - Text color of a participant's bubble.
fires: suggestion-select - The person picked a quick reply.
example:
```html
<wc-chat-message from="participant" author="Priya Shah" channel="Teams"
  datetime="2026-11-08T09:41:00" value="VPN keeps dropping every ten minutes."></wc-chat-message>
```

label: Chat Thread
summary: The scrolling log of a conversation: keeps the latest message in view and announces finished answers.
overview:
Holds wc-chat-messages, oldest first, with wc-chat-event lines between them for what happened along the way. It fills its container and scrolls; while the person reads the end, new messages and growing answers stay in view. Scrolling up stops that, and a Jump to latest button appears.

It is a log (role="log"), but not a live region of its own: streaming text would be read word by word. Instead, an assistant answer or a participant's message is announced once, when it is complete (its streaming turns off), as "Assistant: …".

Before the first message it shows the empty slot and suggestions: prompt starters as chips that fire suggestion-select.
slot: empty - Shown while there are no messages, above the suggestions.
csspart: jump - The Jump to latest button.
cssprop: --chat-thread-padding - Padding of the scrolling area.
fires: suggestion-select - The person picked a prompt starter.
example:

label: Checkbox Group
summary: Groups checkboxes under one label, one name and a list of checked values.
overview:
Checkbox group is the multi-select sibling of wc-radio-group. Its wc-checkbox children are the options: values lists the values of the checked ones, in checkbox order, and value is the same list comma-separated (as on wc-listbox multiple and wc-select multiple), so checkbox values must not contain commas. Setting either checks the matching checkboxes. With no value set, the group adopts the checkboxes checked in markup.

The group is the form control: it submits one entry per checked value under its name, like native checkboxes sharing a name. Its checkboxes do not submit on their own: the group removes their name while they are inside it (and gives it back when one leaves). required blocks form submission until at least one checkbox is checked; disabled and readonly are passed to every checkbox.

select-all adds a parent checkbox above the options that checks or clears every enabled option, and shows the mixed state while only some are checked.

The group has role="group", named by its label; the helper, error or validation text below it is linked with aria-describedby.

```html
  <wc-checkbox value="mentions" label="Mentions"></wc-checkbox>
  <wc-checkbox value="releases" label="Releases"></wc-checkbox>
</wc-checkbox-group>
```

label: Chip
summary: A compact button for an action, a filter or an entered value, with an optional icon and dismiss button.
overview:
A chip is a button, or a link when href is set. The default slot holds the label and the icon slot a leading icon, which a check replaces while the chip is selected. For a read-only status label use wc-tag; to lay chips out or let the person pick from them use wc-chip-set.

With selectable the chip is a toggle (a filter chip) and its button gets aria-pressed from selected. A selecting wc-chip-set sets this and handles the selection; a standalone selectable chip does not toggle itself, so set selected on click. value is what the chip set reports, and defaults to the chip's text.

dismissible adds a close button, labelled from Peacock's strings, that fires dismiss; the chip does not remove itself. disabled turns the chip off; soft-disabled with disabled-reason keeps it focusable and reads the reason to screen readers. skeleton shows a placeholder while the content is not known yet and ignores clicks. tooltip adds a tooltip and throttle-delay throttles clicks.

Without options the chip set only lays its chips out, wrapping them onto new lines.

With selectable it becomes a filter-chip group: a click, Space or Enter on a chip selects it (and again clears it), and value holds the chosen chip's value (or its text). Add multiple to select several; then value is a comma-separated list and values the array. Each change fires change with { value, values? }.

A selecting chip set is one tab stop with role="group"; the arrow keys move between chips (wrapping, mirrored in right-to-left), Home and End jump to the first and last, and every chip is a toggle button with aria-pressed. Name the group with label.

label: Code Editor
summary: A code editor built on Monaco, with syntax highlighting, completions and debugging marks.
overview:
• CodeEditor wraps Monaco Editor as a web component, in the same frame as wc-code-highlighter: an optional header with a title and actions, or a copy button that floats at the top end. Monaco is bundled with Peacock and loaded when the first editor appears; nothing comes from a CDN, so it works under a content security policy that allows only its own origin. The code shows as plain text until Monaco is ready.
  • Its colors come from the theme's color roles and the code highlighter's syntax colors, so light, dark, the system color scheme and custom themes all follow the tokens.
  • Supports TypeScript, JavaScript, JSON, HTML, CSS, SCSS and Markdown, with completions and errors for TypeScript, JavaScript and JSON; read-only mode, line numbers, line wrapping and a minimap.
  • lib-source adds TypeScript declarations for completions, such as the modules a script may import.
  • With breakpoint-gutter, a click in the gutter fires breakpoint-toggle; breakpoints and current-line draw the marks a debugger shows.
  • markers underline problems, such as where a run failed.
  • With fill, the editor drops its frame and takes the height of its container, as a pane of its own.
  • It is a form field: label shows above the editor (and names it for assistive technology), helper-text below it, error with error-text puts it in its error state, and required blocks form submission while it is empty, with the message shown below once the value is committed or the form is submitted.
  • file-name is the header title, such as theme.css.
  • Fires input with { value } on each edit and change with { value } when the editor loses focus after an edit.
  • size sets the size of the code text: sm or md (the default), as on wc-code-highlighter.
  • Line numbers show by default; line-numbers="false" (or the lineNumbers = false property) hides them.

label: Command Palette
summary: A keyboard launcher (Ctrl/Cmd+K) that finds and runs commands by name.
overview:
The command palette is a modal dialog with a search field and a list of commands, grouped under their group headings. It opens in the browser's top layer like wc-modal (scroll lock, Escape, focus return). Commands are data: set commands to an array of {id, label, group, description, icon, shortcut, keywords, disabled}. While the query is empty, the commands whose ids are in recent come first, under "Recent"; the app keeps that list, usually from select.

Typing filters the commands: every word must appear in the label, the keywords or the description, and the matching text is highlighted. Labels that start with the query rank first. With search="managed" the palette does not filter: listen to search, set loading, and replace commands with the results.

The field is an ARIA combobox: focus stays in it while Arrow Up/Down, Home/End and PageUp/PageDown move the highlighted command (aria-activedescendant). Enter runs the highlighted command: select fires, then the palette closes, unless the listener called preventDefault(). Escape first clears the query, then closes.

shortcut opens the palette from anywhere on the page, for example shortcut="mod+k", where mod is Command on Apple platforms and Ctrl elsewhere. The shortcut is ignored while the person types in another field, and closes the palette when it is open.

Ask. With ask, typing offers "Ask the assistant: “…”" too (ADR-030002): first when the query reads like a question or nothing else matches, last otherwise. Choosing it fires a cancelable ask with the query and closes the palette; open the assistant with it. With AI off for the page, the row is not offered.

label: Comment Composer
summary: A box for writing a comment in rich text, with mentions, that sends it with a button or Ctrl+Enter.
overview:
The composer is where people write a comment or a work note, such as at the bottom of a ticket's discussion. It starts as a one-line box; focusing it opens the editor and a footer with the formatting tools and Send. Comments are Markdown: bold, italic, strikethrough, code, links, lists, checklists, quotes and code blocks, but no headings or tables.

Send or Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac) fires a cancelable submit with the Markdown in detail.value and the people it mentions in detail.mentions. Unless the event is cancelled the composer empties; cancel it to keep the text, for example while a request fails. Set loading while the comment is being saved. dismissible adds a Cancel button, and Escape, that empty the composer and fire cancel; use it for reply and edit composers.

Mentions work as on wc-markdown-editor: answer search by setting suggestions. Inside wc-discussion, set the suggestions on the discussion instead and it passes them to whichever composer asked.

Put controls of your own in the footer with the start slot, such as a select for Comment or Work note, or an attach button, and an avatar before the box with the avatar slot. The composer is form-associated, so it also works as the "Additional comments" field of a form.

label: Condition Builder
summary: A query builder for composing filter conditions from rules and nested groups joined by And/Or.
overview:
The condition builder is the root group of a query. It holds rules (wc-cb-rule) and bordered nested groups (wc-cb-group), each joined by a bracket with an And/Or pill.

  • Click the pill to switch a group between And and Or.
  • Drag a rule by its handle to reorder it or move it between groups.
  • Without a mouse, focus a rule's handle: ArrowUp and ArrowDown move it within its group, ArrowRight moves it into the group beside it and ArrowLeft out of its group. Each move is announced.
  • Removing, moving and switching are built in; adding rules and groups is up to you, since only you know what a new rule contains. Listen for add-rule and add-group, which nested groups fire too; detail.group is the group to add to.
  • disabled and readonly apply to every group and rule inside: the add, remove and drag controls are hidden and the operator is locked. Disable or lock the slotted controls yourself.

value (read-only) returns the query as a tree, ready for JSON.stringify():

{
  type: 'group', id, operator: 'and' | 'or', data,
  children: [
    { type: 'rule', id, value, data },
    { type: 'group', id, operator, data, children: [...] }
  ]
}

id is the element's id, data its data-* attributes. A rule's value is the rule's own value property when set, else the values of the controls slotted into it: an object keyed by name when every control has a name, else an array. Each node also has a non-enumerable element, the element it came from, which JSON.stringify() leaves out.

Describe the condition. With a provider that offers parse (ADR-030002), a box above the footer takes a sentence, such as "P1 incidents with no assignment group for over 30 minutes". The provider gets it with target: 'condition-builder' and the fields in ai-schema (never record values), and its answer arrives as describe. Build the rules from it as you build any rule, with suggested on each wc-cb-rule: they show a Suggested badge until the person changes them, and removing one discards it. no-ai turns the box off.
fires: describe - The provider turned the person's sentence into conditions; build the rules from `detail.value`, marked `suggested`.
slot: actions-end - Actions aligned to the end of the footer, such as a "Run query" button.
example:
```html
<wc-condition-builder operator="and">
  <wc-cb-rule>
    <wc-input placeholder="Value"></wc-input>
  </wc-cb-rule>
  <wc-cb-group operator="or">
    <wc-cb-rule>
      <wc-input placeholder="Value"></wc-input>
    </wc-cb-rule>
    <wc-cb-rule>
      <wc-input placeholder="Value"></wc-input>
    </wc-cb-rule>
  </wc-cb-group>
  <wc-button slot="actions-end">Run query</wc-button>
</wc-condition-builder>
```

label: Confirm Dialog
summary: A ready-made "Are you sure?" dialog with confirm and cancel buttons.
overview:
Confirm dialog asks one question before an action runs. It opens in the browser's top layer like wc-modal (same overlay stack: scroll lock, Escape, focus return), with the alertdialog role: the headline is its name and the message its description.

Escape and the cancel button close it; a click on the scrim does not, because a confirmation needs an explicit answer. Set intent="danger" for destructive actions: the confirm button turns the danger color and Cancel gets the initial focus. Set confirm-text to make the person type that text (for example the project name) before Confirm enables.

For an async action, call preventDefault() on confirm: the dialog stays open; set loading while the request runs (the buttons are disabled and Escape does nothing), then call hide(). For a quick question from script, use the confirmDialog() helper, which resolves to true or false.

label: Copy Button
summary: An icon button that copies a value, or the text of another element, to the clipboard.
overview:
Pressing the button copies value, or, without it, the text of the element whose id is in for (the value of an input, textarea or select, else its text content). The element is looked up when the button is pressed, in the same document or shadow root, so its text can change.

It copies with the Clipboard API, and falls back to a hidden textarea and execCommand('copy') where that API is missing or refuses. For about two seconds afterwards the icon turns into a check and the tooltip says "Copied", or into an error icon and "Copy failed"; screen readers hear the same through a polite live region. The accessible name stays label ("Copy" by default) throughout.

The button is a round wc-icon-button and takes its size (default sm) and variant (default text).

label: Currency Field
summary: A field for an amount of money, kept as an exact decimal string in a given currency.
overview:
Currency field takes an amount of money in currency (ISO 4217, such as EUR). Its value is a decimal string with exactly the currency's decimals ("1234.50" for EUR, "1234" for JPY, "1.250" for KWD), or '' while empty, so an amount is never rounded by binary floating point on its way to the server. Inside a <form> that string is submitted under its name.

The currency symbol sits before or after the amount, wherever the locale (the nearest lang, else the browser's) puts it. While the field is not focused the amount shows with grouping (1,234.50); while editing it is plain (1234.50). Typing takes the locale's decimal separator, and pasted amounts such as €1,234.50, 1.234,50 € or (12.00) are read too.

More decimals than the currency has are rejected, not rounded: 1.255 in euros shows "Enter an amount with at most 2 decimal places" and leaves value empty until it is fixed, because silently rounding money changes it. Trailing zeros are fine (1.250 is 1.25). min and max (decimal strings) are compared exactly; with required and text that does not read as an amount they block form submission.

Set currencies to let the person choose the currency: the symbol becomes a currency selector and currency follows it. Every event carries detail.currency.

Currency field or number field? Use wc-number-field with format='{"style":"currency","currency":"EUR"}' when a number that happens to be shown as money is enough: its value is a JavaScript number, it has step and stepper buttons, and the symbol only shows while not editing. Use wc-currency-field for real money: an exact decimal string, decimals that follow the currency, the symbol always in view, pasted formatted amounts, or a currency the person chooses.

Date picker shows a month of days. Pick a day with the pointer or the keyboard; switch to a month or year grid from the header to jump further. With range it picks a start and an end date. It is the calendar inside wc-date-field and can also be placed inline.

label: Dependency map
summary: An explorable map of connected services and assets: service meshes, CMDB relationships, infrastructure.
overview:
Set nodes, edges and optionally groups. Each node has a type, a status (healthy, degraded, down) shown as a ring, and an optional group (a cluster, namespace or business service) drawn as a box. Edges get thicker with traffic (metrics.rps) and warmer with errors (metrics.errorRate); hover one for its metrics. A collapsed group becomes one node with combined status and edges.

layout is force (organic, groups drift together), layered (callers on the left, dependencies on the right) or radial (rings of hops around the focused or selected node). Live updates move as little as possible, and changing layout glides. Drag a node to pin it.

Select a node and set impact to upstream to light up everything that depends on it (what breaks if it goes down), or downstream for everything it depends on; the rest dims. focused-node shows only the nodes within hops of one node (press F on a node). filter limits nodes by type, status, tag or text, and the legend's types toggle it. Zoomed out, nodes become status dots; zoomed in, they show their metrics.

Nodes are buttons with one tab stop. Down moves to a node it depends on, Up to one that depends on it, Left and Right to the other nodes along that step, Enter selects, F focuses and Escape clears. The canvas is infinite like wc-diagram, with the controls and minimap slots.

label: Description Item
summary: One label and its value in a description list.
overview:
Description item is one entry of a wc-description-list: a label ("Status") and its value in the default slot ("Active"). It renders a real <dl> with one <dt> and one <dd>, so a screen reader reads the label as the term and the slotted content as its definition.

An item without a value shows a dash, read as "Not set". The actions slot holds small controls for the value, such as a copy or edit button. span makes the item take a whole row of a multi-column list.

label: Description List
summary: Shows the details of a record as labels and values, such as "Status: Active" and "Owner: Ana".
overview:
Description list lays out wc-description-items, each a label and a value, for record and detail pages. With layout="stacked" (the default) each label sits above its value; with layout="inline" it sits beside it, in a column of the same width for every item, so the values line up.

columns (1 to 4) puts the items in a grid. The grid follows the width of the list, not of the window: below 40rem it drops to at most two columns and below 24rem to one, where inline items also stack. divided draws a line under every item. An item with span takes a whole row.

Each item is its own <dl> with a <dt> and a <dd>, so screen readers announce every label as the term of its value.

label: Diagram
summary: An infinite canvas of nodes and connections that the person pans, zooms and edits, for state machines, process maps and node editors.
overview:
Set nodes and edges as properties. A node shows a built-in card with headline, supportingText and icon, or your own content in an element with slot="node:<id>". Nodes connect through ports on their sides; edges are drawn as rounded elbows by default (connector), with an optional label and markers at each end.

The canvas is infinite: drag the background, hold Space and drag, use the middle button or a trackpad to pan, and hold Ctrl or Command and scroll, or pinch, to zoom. It opens at start-position (fit, origin or first) or at an exact start-view; Home or home() flies back there, Shift+1 or fit() fits all content, and a "Back to content" button appears when everything is out of view. Read and set the camera with view, and save it from viewport-change. Add wc-diagram-controls and wc-diagram-minimap in the controls and minimap slots.

By default nodes can be dragged and connections drawn; the diagram fires node-drag-end and connect and leaves edges to you. editable turns it into a full editor: it adds the edge on connect unless you cancel the event, selects edges, draws a marquee with Shift + drag, moves several nodes at once, snaps to other nodes (and to the grid with snap-to-grid), deletes with Delete, copies and pastes, and undoes with Ctrl+Z. Every committed edit fires change. readonly keeps everything in place.

The diagram never mutates the objects you pass: edits assign new nodes and edges arrays. Each node is focusable and named by its headline. Arrow keys move the focused node by 20px (Shift: 100px), Alt + arrow moves focus to the nearest node in that direction, and Enter or Space selects it. Arrow keys follow the canvas axes and are not mirrored in right-to-left layouts.

This component was called wc-flow before 4.0. That tag still works as a deprecated alias until 5.0.

label: Diagram controls
summary: Zoom, fit, back-to-start and undo buttons for a diagram canvas such as `wc-diagram`.
overview:
Put it in a canvas's controls slot, or anywhere on the page with for set to the canvas's id. It shows zoom out, the zoom level, zoom in, fit to content and back to start; undo and redo join them when the canvas is editable. The zoom level opens a menu with 50%, 100%, 200%, fit, zoom to selection and back to start.

It is a toolbar: Tab reaches it once and the arrow keys move between its buttons.

label: Diff Viewer
summary: Shows what changed between two texts, such as two versions of a config or document.
overview:
The viewer compares old-value and new-value line by line (Myers' algorithm) and marks the changed words inside each pair of changed lines. A summary such as "3 additions, 2 deletions" sits at the top. Unchanged lines more than context lines (default 3) away from a change fold into a "Show 24 unchanged lines" button that expands them.

view="unified" (the default) lists removed lines before the added lines that replace them, with old and new line numbers; view="split" puts the old text on the left and the new text on the right (code reads left to right, also in right-to-left pages).

Lines are compared without their line endings, so CRLF and LF texts match; a note says when the endings differ. A last line without a line break is marked when the other side has one. Texts that are too different or too large to compare line by line within a time budget are shown as the changed part removed and then added, with a note.

The diff is a table: each row is a line, removed and added lines carry a − or + marker besides their color, and screen readers hear "Removed line 12" or "Added line 13" before the text. The text is shown plain, without syntax highlighting.

label: Discussion
summary: The discussion of a record, such as a ticket: comments with replies, activity entries and a rich-text composer with mentions.
overview:
A discussion holds wc-discussion-comment and wc-discussion-activity elements in the order the app gives them (oldest or newest first), and a wc-comment-composer under them. The app owns the data: it renders the entries and changes them in answer to the events, which all bubble, so one listener on the discussion hears them.

  • submit (cancelable) with { value, mentions, parentId }: a new comment from the composer (parentId null) or a reply. Cancel it to keep the text in the composer.
  • edit (cancelable), delete, reply and copy-link, from the comments.
  • search with { trigger, query } from any composer, the main one or a reply or edit composer. Answer by setting suggestions (and suggestions-loading) on the discussion; it passes them to the composer that asked.

Put your own wc-comment-composer in the composer slot to add footer controls (a Comment / Work note select, an attach button) or an avatar. readonly hides the composer, Reply and Edit. triggers and mention-href pass down to every comment and composer. loading shows placeholder rows; without entries the discussion says "No comments yet" (replace it with the empty slot). The header slot sits above the entries, for a title, a count or a sort control.

Accessibility: the entries sit in a role="feed" named by label ("Comments" by default). Page Down and Page Up move focus between entries and Ctrl+End to the composer. A comment added after the discussion has loaded is announced politely.
slot: empty - Replaces the "No comments yet" message.
fires: submit - Cancelable. A new comment or a reply.
example:
```html
<wc-discussion>
  <wc-discussion-activity author="Ana Lima" datetime="2026-11-07T08:00:00Z" value="opened the ticket"></wc-discussion-activity>
  <wc-discussion-comment comment-id="1" author="Ravi Kumar" datetime="2026-11-07T09:30:00Z" value="Looking into it."></wc-discussion-comment>
</wc-discussion>
```

label: Discussion Comment
summary: One comment in a discussion: author, time, Markdown text, actions, replies and inline reply and edit.
overview:
A comment shows its author (with a wc-avatar from avatar-src, or initials), its time and its text. value is Markdown, shown with wc-markdown, so mentions show as chips. datetime (ISO 8601) shows relative to now and keeps itself current; with href (the comment's permalink) the time links to it. edited adds an "Edited" marker, and the badge slot holds a tag such as Work note.

Replies are wc-discussion-comment elements with slot="replies", one level deep. Reply fires a cancelable reply and opens a wc-comment-composer under the replies; sending it fires submit with detail.parentId set to this comment's comment-id. Edit (with editable) turns the text into a composer; saving fires a cancelable edit with the new Markdown. Cancel either event to keep the composer open, for example while a save fails. Delete (with deletable) and Copy link (with href) fire delete and copy-link. The app owns the data: it updates value, adds the reply, or removes the comment.

Use comments inside wc-discussion, which passes down readonly, triggers and mention-href, and gives the reply and edit composers their mention suggestions.
slot: replies - The replies: `wc-discussion-comment` elements.
fires: copy-link - The person chose Copy link; the link is on the clipboard.
example:
```html

  value="Restarted the worker. [@Ravi Kumar](mention:usr_7), can you check?"></wc-discussion-comment>
```

label: Document Editor
summary: A word-processor style editor with pages, a header and footer, page numbers, tables, images and an outline.
overview:
Use it for long, structured documents that are read as pages: policies, contracts, reports, specifications. The text flows over pages of the chosen size, A4, Letter or Legal, portrait or landscape, with normal, narrow or wide margins. Paragraphs continue on the next page at the line that does not fit; tables break between rows; images move whole. Ctrl/Cmd+Enter inserts a page break.

Double-click the top or bottom margin of a page to edit the header or footer, which repeat on every page; the toolbar then inserts the page number or page count. The outline lists the headings for navigation (outline-open), and the status bar shows the page setup, word count and the current page. print() prints the pages as they look, always at 100%.

Zoom. By default (zoom="fit") a page wider than the editor is scaled down to fit its width, so narrow containers, tablets and phones show whole pages instead of scrolling sideways; it is never enlarged past 100%. Set zoom to a percentage, or pick one in the status bar, to show the pages at a fixed size; the editor fires zoom-change when the person changes it. Zooming only changes how the pages are shown: the text flows over the same pages at every zoom.

The value is a DocumentValue: the page setup and the body, header and footer as Tiptap JSON, so alignment, colors and page setup are kept. getMarkdown() and getHTML() export the body. The editor fires input with { value } as the document changes (after debounce milliseconds) and change when focus leaves after an edit.

Images. Inserting an image (toolbar, paste or drop) fires image-upload with the file and a respond(src, alt?) function. Store the file and call respond with its address; Peacock never uploads anything itself, and does not embed files in the value.

Mentions work as on wc-markdown-editor: answer search by setting suggestions.

Comments. Comment (toolbar or selection bubble) highlights the selected text and fires a cancelable comment-add with a new threadId and the quote. The app owns the threads: it puts an element per thread in the comments slot with a thread-id attribute, usually a wc-discussion, and the editor lines each one up beside its text in a column next to the pages. The thread under the caret gets data-active and fires comment-select; focusing a thread highlights its text. removeComment() clears a resolved thread's highlight, focusComment() goes to it, and comments lists them. The highlights are part of the document, so they are shared when collaborating.

Collaboration. Set collaboration to { document, provider, user }: a Y.Doc, its provider (any Yjs provider; its awareness carries carets and presence) and the person editing here. Everyone's edits, the header, footer and page setup merge live; other people's carets show with their names, and their avatars appear in the toolbar (presence-change lists them). Edits from others update value without firing input. The first person into an empty shared document brings this editor's value. Collaboration needs the yjs package, which loads only when it is used.

label: Draft Card
summary: A record the assistant prepared, shown for the person to confirm, edit in the app's form, or discard.
overview:
The only way the assistant's writes appear (ADR-000007: reads are free, writes are drafts). headline says what it is ("New incident") and supporting-text where ("IT service desk"); put the app's mark in the start slot. List the values in fields, each optionally suggested with a reason, or slot your own content.

The buttons fire events; the app does the work and sets state:

  • confirm (the confirm-label button, such as "Raise incident"): set submitting, then done with result-text and result-href, or error with error-text.
  • edit (Edit in form): open the app's own form, filled with the draft, for example with wc-form's suggest().
  • discard: the card turns discarded unless the event is cancelled.

With irreversible, Confirm asks again in a wc-confirm-dialog first. Like every marker of the assistant, the card renders nothing while AI is off for the page.

label: Elevation
summary: A shadow layer placed inside an element to lift it off the page, with a shadow depth set per level and per side.
overview:
• Elevation adds a shadow effect to an element to give it depth.
  • It can be used to create a sense of hierarchy or to draw attention to a particular element.
  • It fills its nearest positioned ancestor, so place it inside an element with position: relative. It ignores pointer events.
  • --elevation-level sets the level. --elevation-level-block-start, --elevation-level-block-end, --elevation-level-inline-start and --elevation-level-inline-end set the level of one side and override --elevation-level for it; the inline sides follow the reading direction.

label: ERD
summary: An entity-relationship diagram: tables with their columns, joined by crow's-foot relations.
overview:
Set entities (each with columns) and relations. A relation runs from the entity holding the foreign key (source, sourceColumn) to the one it references (target, targetColumn), and its ends show crow's-foot cardinality (many to one by default). Lines join the column rows and route at right angles. Primary keys show a key, foreign keys a link. Hover an entity or a column to highlight what it is joined to.

Entities without a position are laid out automatically: referenced tables to the left of the tables that reference them. Collapse an entity to its header with the chevron (or Shift+Enter); the layout closes the gap. schema shows one schema, and focused-node with hops shows one entity's neighbourhood (press F on an entity). Zoomed far out, rows become bars.

With editable: double-click a name or type to rename it (F2 on an entity), add and remove columns, click a row's key to toggle the primary key, drag the ring at a row's end onto another row to add a relation and pick its cardinality, and delete with Delete. Every edit fires change with the new entities and relations; undo with Ctrl+Z.

Entities are one tab stop: arrow keys move to the nearest entity in that direction, Enter selects. The canvas is infinite like wc-diagram, with the controls and minimap slots.
